analysis.one_liner: Sets a strict national limit for lead in tap water and makes water systems replace lead pipes and warn residents.
analysis.headline: Introduced in July 1991 with one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor, the bill never received a committee markup or a floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have written a lead rule directly into the Safe Drinking Water Act, replacing a regulation the EPA issued in May 1991 that environmental groups considered too weak. It set a hard limit of 10 parts per billion of lead at the tap, declared the health goal for lead to be zero, and required water systems that exceed the limit to treat their water to reduce corrosion, replace lead service lines, and tell customers plainly what is in their water. It also required schools to test their drinking water and banned the sale of plumbing materials containing lead.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who drinks tap water, especially children and pregnant women in homes with lead pipes, lead solder, or lead service lines. The bill required water systems exceeding the limit to run corrosion-control treatment [S2], replace lead service lines at 20 percent per year [S2], and deliver public education materials in the languages their communities speak [S2]. It required schools to test their drinking water and tell parents and staff when lead was found [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Establishes a hard limit of 10 parts per billion of lead at the tap, with the national health goal for lead set at zero, replacing the EPA rule issued May 6, 1991; the EPA could issue lead rules only if more protective than the bill's [S2][S3]
Requires systems that exceed the limit to install corrosion-control treatment, which coats pipes so lead stops dissolving into drinking water, on fixed deadlines by system size [S2][S3]

Requires systems that still exceed the limit to replace lead service lines at an annual rate of 20 percent of lead lines or 10 percent of all lines, whichever is greater, and presumes the utility controls the whole line unless it proves otherwise [S2][S3]

Requires systems exceeding the limit to send customers detailed health warnings in water bills, newspapers, schools, clinics, and broadcast announcements, in the appropriate languages where many residents do not speak English [S2][S3]
Requires local school systems to test drinking water from coolers and other outlets, disclose results to parents and staff, and face civil penalties for failing to test and fix contamination [S2][S3]

Bans selling pipes, fittings, fixtures, solder, or flux that are not lead-free, and redefines 'lead-free' four years after enactment to mean no lead content at all, tighter than the 8 percent limit then allowed for faucets and pipes [S2][S3]
Requires systems exceeding the limit to offer to sample any customer's tap water on request, and requires bottled water supply as a condition of some variances where a health risk remains [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Public water systems would bear the cost of monitoring every six months, corrosion-control studies and treatment, public education campaigns, and replacing lead service lines; those costs largely flow to ratepayers through water bills. Plumbing manufacturers would bear the cost of reformulating pipes, fittings, fixtures, solder, and flux to contain no lead. Building owners whose portion of a lead service line the utility does not control would still be offered replacement at their own expense.

drawbacks.text: The compliance costs are substantial: corrosion-control studies and treatment, six-month tap monitoring, reporting and recordkeeping, and replacing lead service lines at up to 20 percent a year all fall on water systems, and utilities generally recover such costs from customers through rates [S2][S3]

A single tap sample above 10 parts per billion counts as an exceedance, a stricter trigger than a typical averaging rule, which would push more systems into replacement and education programs and raise costs [S3]

When a utility controls only part of a lead service line, it may replace just its portion and leave the owner's section in place; replacing only part of a lead line is known from plumbing practice to sometimes disturb the pipe and temporarily raise lead levels at the tap, though the bill requires the system to offer a follow-up sample within 14 days [S3]

The bill imposes heavy paperwork: materials evaluations, targeted sampling-site pools, water-quality parameter monitoring, and annual compliance certifications from every system, which small systems in particular would struggle to administer [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health stakes are high and one-sided: no level of lead exposure is known to be safe, children's developmental damage from lead is irreversible, and drinking water was estimated to supply about a fifth of a person's lead exposure [S3]. The bill's costs fall mainly on utilities and ratepayers and on plumbing manufacturers, and a hard 10 ppb limit triggered by any single sample is an aggressive design that would have been expensive to run. On balance, the bill traded real, ongoing compliance costs for reducing a well-documented poison in drinking water, and it aimed at a stronger standard than the EPA rule already in place.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Frank Lautenberg introduced the bill on July 10, 1991, joined by Sen. Dave Durenberger and Sen. Joseph Lieberman, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day [S1][S3][S5]
The bill had two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat [S4]
No further action was ever taken: the committee never scheduled a markup or reported the bill, and no floor vote occurred before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5]

The bill would have superseded the EPA's May 6, 1991 lead rule, which relied on an 'action level' approach the bill's authors replaced with a firm maximum contaminant level of 10 parts per billion [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Public water systems and plumbing-materials makers avoided the new monitoring, treatment, replacement, and lead-free product costs. People drinking tap water, especially children in older homes with lead plumbing, continued to rely on the EPA rule the bill would have replaced.

for.role: U.S. Senator from New Jersey; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Lead in Drinking Water Reduction Act of 1991 on July 10, 1991

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat with a Republican and another Democratic cosponsor — but no roll-call vote was ever taken, so the partisan split on the merits is unknown.

industries.note: The bill required corrosion-control treatment on fixed deadlines, tap monitoring every six months, public education campaigns, and replacement of lead service lines at up to 20 percent per year for systems exceeding the 10 ppb limit; utilities generally pass these compliance costs to customers through water bills.

industries.industry: Pipe, fitting, fixture, solder and flux manufacturers
industries.note: Four years after enactment, 'lead-free' would mean zero lead content, and selling non-lead-free plumbing materials for drinking-water use would become unlawful — tighter than the 8 percent lead content then allowed in faucets and pipes.
Mandatory tap, source-water, and water-quality-parameter monitoring on six-month cycles, plus school testing, would create steady demand for certified labs.
